lessons.title: Listening for TCP connections
lessons.book_section: 21.1 Building a Single-Threaded Web Server: Listening to the TCP Connection
lessons.objective_md: Bind a `TcpListener`, accept connections, and understand what a connection is.

screens.heading: A listener
screens.text_md:
A web server's first job is to **listen** for connections. `TcpListener::bind` claims an address and **port** (`127.0.0.1:7878`); `127.0.0.1` means "this computer only". `incoming()` is an iterator of connection attempts: each item is a `TcpStream`, an open two-way connection, or an error.

When `_stream` goes out of scope, the connection is closed.

coming_from.c: It wraps `socket`, `bind`, `listen` and `accept`, closing the socket on drop.
coming_from.js: Like `net.createServer(...).listen(7878)`, but the loop is yours instead of an event callback.
coming_from.python: Like `socket.socket()`, `bind`, `listen` and `accept()` in a loop, wrapped into one `TcpListener`.

screens.heading: Port 0 and the real address
screens.text_md: Binding to port **0** asks the operating system for any free port; `local_addr()` says which one it picked. That's how tests run servers without clashing. `accept()` waits for one connection and also returns the client's address. Here a second thread plays the client.

screens.heading: A port already in use
screens.text_md: Only one listener can own an address at a time. Binding can also fail for ports below 1024, which need administrator rights on many systems. That's why `bind` returns a `Result`: real servers report the error instead of crashing.

screens.heading: Attempts, not requests
screens.text_md: Each item of `incoming()` is a connection *attempt*, not an HTTP request: a browser may open several connections, and some attempts fail. `take(3)` makes the loop finite, which is how the course's servers and tests stop.

screens.heading: TCP is a byte stream
screens.text_md: TCP delivers bytes in order, but not in "messages": two writes may arrive as one read, or one write as several reads. A protocol on top, like HTTP, decides where a request ends. `read_to_string` reads until the other side closes the connection.

lessons.title: Reading requests and writing responses
lessons.book_section: 21.1 Reading the Request; Writing a Response; Returning Real HTML
lessons.objective_md: Read an HTTP request's header lines and write a correctly framed response.

screens.heading: What a request looks like
screens.text_md:
An HTTP request is text. The first line is the **request line**: method, path, version. Header lines follow, each ending with `\r\n` (CRLF), and an empty line ends the header. `lines()` strips the line endings, so the empty line is an empty string, where `take_while` stops.

A `Cursor` over a string behaves like a stream here; the Book reads from a `TcpStream` the same way.

coming_from.c: Like `recv` into a buffer and splitting on `\r\n`, with buffering done by `BufReader`.
coming_from.java: Like reading a `BufferedReader` over the socket's input stream until an empty line.
coming_from.js: Node's `http` module parses this for you; here you see the raw text.
coming_from.python: Like reading `sock.makefile()` line by line, what `http.server` does for you.

screens.heading: Bounded reading
screens.text_md: A client controls how much it sends, so a server must bound what it reads, or one request could use unlimited memory. `take(8192)` wraps a reader so it stops after 8192 bytes; `read_line` then returns at most that much even if no newline came.

question.prompt_md: How does a server know where an HTTP request's header ends?

explanations.text_md: Correct. A blank line separates the header from any body.
Not quite. The client waits for the reply with the connection open.
Not quite. Headers vary in length.
Not quite. That ends only the first line.

screens.heading: Writing a response
screens.text_md: A response mirrors a request: a **status line** (`HTTP/1.1 200 OK`), headers, an empty line, then the body. **`Content-Length`** tells the client how many bytes of body to read, so it must be the body's length in **bytes**, which `String::len` gives. (The `⏎` marks the CRLFs in this printout.)

screens.heading: `write_all`
screens.text_md: `write` may accept only part of the buffer and tell you how much; sockets do this when their buffers fill up. **`write_all`** keeps calling `write` until every byte is out. Always use it to send a response.

question.prompt_md: For the body `"é"`, the correct header is `Content-Length: 1`.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `é` is two bytes in UTF-8.
Correct. `Content-Length` counts bytes: `2`.

screens.heading: A full exchange
screens.text_md: Both sides together: the client sends a request and **half-closes** its write side (`shutdown(Shutdown::Write)`) to say "that's all", then reads the reply to the end. The server reads the request line, answers with `write_all`, and closes the connection by dropping the stream.

A response is a status line, headers (including a byte-exact `Content-Length`), an empty line and the body.
Send with `write_all`, never a single `write`.

screens.text_md: Handling each request on its own thread lets the fast one finish while the slow one sleeps. The fix, next lesson, is a **thread pool**: a fixed number of threads that take turns.

lessons.title: Designing a thread pool
lessons.book_section: 21.2 Turning Our Single-Threaded Server into a Multithreaded Server: Improving Throughput with a Thread Pool
lessons.objective_md: Design the `ThreadPool` interface: its constructor, `execute`, and the bounds a job needs.

screens.heading: Interface first
screens.text_md: The Book designs the pool from the code that will use it: `ThreadPool::new(4)` then `pool.execute(|| …)` for each connection, mirroring `thread::spawn`. This first version just runs the job immediately, but the interface is final, so the server code won't change when the real pool arrives.

coming_from.c: Like a hand-written pool around `std::thread` and a task queue.
coming_from.go: Like a fixed number of goroutines reading jobs from a channel.
coming_from.js: Like a worker pool library (`piscina`) with a `run(task)` method.

screens.heading: Why `FnOnce() + Send + 'static`
screens.text_md:
The bounds on `execute` are copied from `thread::spawn`, because each job will run on another thread:

- **`FnOnce()`**: the job runs once, so it may consume what it captured.
- **`Send`**: it can move to another thread.
- **`'static`**: it borrows nothing that might end before the thread runs it.

options.text_md: The job will be moved to a worker thread.
The job must return a value.
So the job can be called many times.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Only `Send` values may cross threads.
Not quite. Jobs return `()`.
Not quite. That would be `Fn`.
Not quite. It's about safety.

screens.heading: Validating the size
screens.text_md: A pool with zero threads could never run anything. The Book's `new` panics on zero, which suits a size fixed in the code; it suggests a `build` that returns a `Result` for sizes that come from input. Both make an empty pool impossible to create.

screens.heading: Workers, not threads
screens.text_md: The standard library can't spawn a thread and hand it code *later*: `spawn` needs the closure up front. So the pool keeps **workers**, each owning a thread that will wait for jobs. A `Worker` with an `id` is also easier to log and debug than a bare handle.

screens.heading: A plan before the pool
screens.text_md: It helps to reason about the pool before building it. With a round-robin plan, seven jobs on three workers go to `0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0`. The real pool will be more flexible: whichever worker is free takes the next job.

lessons.title: Workers and jobs
lessons.book_section: 21.2 Creating a Finite Number of Threads; Sending Requests to Threads via Channels
lessons.objective_md: Connect workers to the pool with a channel of boxed jobs, shared through `Arc<Mutex<…>>`.

screens.heading: A channel of jobs
screens.text_md: Each closure has its own type, so jobs travel as a trait object: **`Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>`**, named `Job`. The pool holds the **sender**; the workers will share the **receiver**. Calling a boxed `FnOnce` runs it and uses it up.

coming_from.go: Exactly the Go idiom: a `chan func()` read by worker goroutines.
coming_from.js: Like posting tasks to a worker's message queue.
coming_from.python: Like a `queue.Queue` of callables that worker threads `get()` from.

screens.heading: One receiver, many workers
screens.text_md: A channel has many senders but **one** receiver (**E0382** when two threads try to own it). To share it, wrap it: **`Arc<Mutex<Receiver<Job>>>`**. `Arc` lets every worker own a handle; `Mutex` lets one worker at a time receive.

screens.heading: The worker loop
screens.text_md:
Each worker loops: lock the receiver, `recv` one job, run it. When the sender is dropped and the queue is empty, `recv` returns `Err` and the loop ends. Which worker runs which job varies, but all six run.

The lock and `recv` are in one `let` statement: the guard is a temporary dropped at the `;`, **before** the job runs.

lessons.title: Graceful shutdown
lessons.objective_md: Shut the pool down cleanly: close the channel, let workers finish, and join them in `Drop`.

screens.heading: Joining needs ownership
screens.text_md: `join` takes the `JoinHandle` by value, but `Drop::drop` gets only `&mut self` (**E0507**). The fix is the same trick as the blog's state: store `Option<JoinHandle<()>>` and `take()` it out.

error[E0507]: cannot move out of `worker.thread` which is behind a mutable reference
  --> src/main.rs:14:13
   |
14 |             worker.thread.join().expect("no panic");
   |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ------ `worker.thread` moved due to this method call
   |             |
   |             move occurs because `worker.thread` has type `JoinHandle<()>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait

annotations.mark: `worker.thread` moved due to this method call
annotations.note_md: line 14: `join` consumes the handle, but `drop` only has `&mut self`.

screens.heading: `take` the handle
screens.text_md: `Option::take` moves the handle out and leaves `None`, so `join` can consume it. A second `drop` (or a second shutdown call) finds `None` and does nothing.

coming_from.c: Like a destructor that signals the queue and joins every `std::thread` (as `std::jthread` does).
coming_from.go: Like closing the jobs channel and waiting on a `sync.WaitGroup`.
coming_from.java: Like `shutdown()` followed by `awaitTermination()`, triggered by `Drop` instead of a `finally`.
coming_from.js: Like awaiting every worker's termination in a cleanup handler.
coming_from.python: Like `executor.shutdown(wait=True)`, run automatically when the pool goes out of scope.

question.prompt_md: Why is the worker's handle stored as `Option<JoinHandle<()>>`?

options.text_md: So `drop` can `take()` it and call `join`, which needs ownership.
Because a worker may have no thread at all.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `take` moves it out through `&mut self`.
Not quite. Every worker has a thread until it's joined.
Not quite. `Option` doesn't make it `Copy`.
Not quite. It can; joining from `drop` is the problem.

screens.heading: Close the channel first
screens.text_md: Joining a worker that's waiting in `recv` would wait forever. So shutdown first **drops the sender**: once the queued jobs are taken, `recv` returns `Err`, the worker's loop breaks, and its thread ends. Then `join` returns. The pool keeps the sender in an `Option` too, so `drop` can take it.

question.prompt_md: Dropping the sender throws away jobs that are already queued.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Queued jobs are still received; `recv` fails only when the queue is empty.
Correct. Workers drain the queue, then stop.

screens.heading: The order matters
screens.text_md:
Graceful shutdown is a sequence:

1. Drop the sender (`drop(self.sender.take())`), closing the channel.
2. Each worker keeps taking jobs until the queue is empty.
3. `recv` returns `Err`, and each worker's loop ends.
4. `Drop` joins every worker, in order.

Join first and the program hangs, because workers never learn there's no more work.

screens.text_md: The Book's final server serves two requests (`incoming().take(2)`) and then lets the pool go out of scope, which runs `Drop`: the channel closes, workers finish, and every thread is joined before `main` returns. Finite servers like this are also what make the course's tests reliable.

- `read_head(reader)`: reads lines from any `BufRead` until the empty line and returns them without their line endings (`\r\n`, or a bare `\n`). problems.title: Dispatch owned jobs to fixed workers
problems.description_md:
Build the Book's `ThreadPool`: a fixed set of worker threads that run jobs sent to them.

- `ThreadPool::new(size)` creates a channel, wraps the receiver in `Arc<Mutex<…>>`, and starts `size` workers that share it. (A size of 0 is a bug in the caller: `assert!` it.)
- Each `Worker` runs a loop: lock the receiver, `recv()` one job, **release the lock**, run the job. When `recv` fails (the channel is closed), the loop ends.
- `execute(f)` boxes the closure as a `Job` (`Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>`) and sends it.
- `size()` is the number of workers.

Write the lock and `recv` in one `let` statement so the guard is dropped before the job runs; otherwise one long job would block every other worker. Shutdown comes in P21-07; here the workers simply keep waiting.

```text
Expression: { let (tx, rx) = std::sync::mpsc::channel(); let pool = crate::ThreadPool::new(3); for i in 0..5 { let tx = tx.clone(); pool.execute(move || tx.send(i * i).expect("sent")); } drop(tx); let mut v: Vec<i32> = rx.iter().collect(); v.sort(); v }
```

- `stop()` (private): drop the sender (take it out of its `Option`), which closes the channel. Each worker finishes the jobs already queued, then its `recv` fails and its loop ends. problems.title: Serve a finite loopback HTTP workload
problems.description_md:
Put it all together: `serve(listener, workers, max_requests)` accepts exactly `max_requests` connections (counting every accepted connection, even malformed ones), hands each to a `ThreadPool` of `workers` threads, waits for them all (drop the pool) and returns how many it accepted.

Each connection is handled by reading the request line (at most 8192 bytes), reading and discarding the rest of what the client sent (up to 1 MB; the clients close their write side, so this ends), and writing one response before closing:

| Request line | Response |
|---|---|
| `GET / HTTP/1.1` | `200 OK`, body `Hello!` |
| `GET /echo/WORD HTTP/1.1` | `200 OK`, body `WORD` |
| other `GET … HTTP/1.1` | `404 Not Found`, body `Not found` |
| anything else, or a line that can't be read | `400 Bad Request`, body `Bad request` |

Every response is `HTTP/1.1 STATUS REASON\r\nContent-Length: N\r\n\r\nBODY`. The starter includes the finished `ThreadPool` from P21-07 and a test client, `fetch(port, raw)`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let l = std::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").expect("bind"); let port = l.local_addr().expect("addr").port(); let server = std::thread::spawn(move || crate::serve(l, 2, 1).map_err(|e| e.to_string())); let r = crate::fetch(port, "GET / HTTP/1.1

").map_err(|e| e.to_string()); let n = server.join().expect("no panic"); (r, n) }
Expected:   (Ok("HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 6

Hello!"), Ok(1))
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 64 workers and 200 requests per test.
- No `unsafe`.
- No `unwrap()`.
hints: `for stream in listener.incoming().take(max_requests) { let stream = stream?; pool.execute(move || { let _ = handle(stream); }); }`

With `let mut reader = BufReader::new(&mut stream);`, `(&mut reader).take(8192).read_line(&mut line)` reads at most 8192 bytes of the first line, and `io::copy(&mut (&mut reader).take(1 << 20), &mut io::sink())` discards the rest.
Reuse the routing from P21-04 as a `match` on the line's words, and `write_all` the formatted response.
problems.solution_approach_md: `incoming().take(n)` turns the endless stream of connections into exactly `n`, so the server ends by itself. Each connection becomes a job; dropping the pool afterwards waits for every job, so when `serve` returns, every client has its full reply. Reading through `take(8192)` bounds how much of a hostile request is read.
problems.idiomatic_md: Finite servers (`take(n)`) make network code testable: the test can join the server thread and know all the work is done.

problems.description_md:
Build the Book's final project, a small multithreaded web server, in the library package `hello`. It speaks a deliberately small subset of HTTP/1.1: one request line per connection, one response, then the connection closes.

**Part 1 · Routes and responses**

`respond(request_line, slow)` returns `(status, reason, body)`: `GET /` gives `(200, "OK", "Hello!")`; `GET /sleep` sleeps for `slow` and gives `(200, "OK", "Slept")`; `GET /echo/WORD` gives `(200, "OK", "WORD")`; any other `GET … HTTP/1.1` gives `(404, "Not Found", "Not found")`; everything else `(400, "Bad Request", "Bad request")`. `format_response(status, reason, body)` builds `HTTP/1.1 STATUS REASON\r\nContent-Length: N\r\n\r\nBODY` with `N` in bytes.

**Part 2 · The thread pool**

`ThreadPool::new(size)` starts `size` workers sharing a job channel through `Arc<Mutex<…>>`; `execute(f)` sends a boxed `FnOnce() + Send + 'static` job; `size()` reports the workers. `shutdown(self)` and `Drop` close the channel, let the workers finish every queued job, join them, and (for `shutdown`) return the joined worker IDs in order.

**Part 3 · Serving**

`serve(listener, workers, max_requests, slow)` accepts exactly `max_requests` connections, hands each to the pool, waits for all of them and returns the count. Each connection reads the request line (at most 8192 bytes), discards the rest of the request (up to 1 MB), and writes the response with `write_all`. A test client, `fetch(port, raw)`, is given.
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 64 workers and 200 requests per test.
- No `unsafe`, no `unwrap()`.
hints: Part 1 is a `match` on the line's words as a slice, as in P21-04.
Part 2 is P21-06 plus P21-07: workers lock, `recv`, release, run; `Drop` takes the sender and joins every worker.
Part 3 is P21-08 with the `slow` duration passed through to `respond`.
problems.solution_approach_md: The routes are a pure function, easy to test without sockets. The pool turns each connection into a job for a fixed set of threads, so a slow request occupies one worker while the others keep serving. `incoming().take(n)` makes the server finite, and dropping the pool waits for every job, so `serve` returns only after every client has its reply.
problems.idiomatic_md: In production you'd use an async runtime or a library such as `hyper`; building the pool by hand shows what those libraries do for you.

problems.description_md:
The library gets a read-only web front end. The starter is the LM20 workspace with one new module, `core/src/web.rs` (`pub mod web;` is already in `core/src/lib.rs`), which includes a test client, `fetch(port, raw)`.

**Part 1 · Routes**

`respond(lib, request_line)` returns `(status, body)` for `GET … HTTP/1.1` requests (anything else is `(400, "Bad request")`):

| Path | Response |
|---|---|
| `/health` | `(200, "ok")` |
| `/books` | `200`, each book's `summary()` followed by `\n`, in catalogue order |
| `/authors` | `200`, each author from `authors()` followed by `\n` |
| `/books/ID`, `ID` all decimal digits | `200` and the book's summary plus `\n`, or `(404, "No such book")` when there's no such book or the number doesn't fit a `u32` |
| anything else | `(404, "Not found")` |

**Part 2 · Serving**

`serve(lib, listener, workers, max_requests)` shares the library between connections as `Arc<Mutex<Library>>`, handles each of exactly `max_requests` connections on its own thread with at most `workers` running at once (join the oldest before starting another), joins them all, and returns the count. Each handler reads the request line (at most 8192 bytes), discards the rest, computes the response **while holding the lock**, releases it, then writes `HTTP/1.1 STATUS REASON\r\nContent-Length: N\r\n\r\nBODY` (`OK`, `Not Found` or `Bad Request`). No route changes the library.

```text

Expected:   (200, "Dune by Frank Herbert (1965)\n")
```

hints: `let ["GET", path, "HTTP/1.1"] = words.as_slice() else { return (400, …); };` then match `path.split('/')` as a slice: `["", "books", id] if …`.
`id.parse::<u32>().ok().and_then(|n| lib.book(n))` handles both a missing book and a number that's too large.
In `handle`, build the response inside a block that holds the lock guard, so the guard is dropped before `write_all`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Routing is a slice pattern over the path's segments, with a guard that accepts only decimal IDs, so `/books/x` falls through to *Not found* while `/books/99` is *No such book*. The library is behind `Arc<Mutex<…>>` because handlers run on several threads; holding the lock only while computing the response keeps slow clients from blocking the others.
